nameStory: The corrugated-cap milky gets its name from its distinctive wrinkled cap surface that looks like corrugated cardboard or a washboard. Like all milkcaps, when you cut or break this mushroom, it 'bleeds' a milky white latex that oozes from the damaged tissue.
description: The corrugated-cap milky is a medium to large mushroom with a distinctive wrinkled, bumpy cap that immediately catches the eye. Its most famous feature is the white, milky liquid that flows out when you cut or damage any part of the mushroom. The cap ranges from tan to reddish-brown, often with darker zones, and sits atop a sturdy, pale stem. These mushrooms can grow quite substantial, with caps reaching 3-6 inches across.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Deeply wrinkled and corrugated like cardboard, with a bumpy, uneven surface that feels rough to the touch. Color ranges from tan to reddish-brown with darker concentric zones.

idTips.label: Milk/Latex
idTips.description: White milky liquid oozes out immediately when cap, gills, or stem are cut or damaged. The latex doesn't change color and tastes mild to slightly bitter.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Pale cream to buff colored, running slightly down the stem. They feel brittle and snap cleanly when bent, and also release white milk when damaged.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick and sturdy, pale tan to whitish, often with shallow pits or depressions scattered across the surface. No ring present.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White to pale cream colored when collected on dark paper over several hours.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, fruity aroma that some describe as apricot-like or sweet. The smell becomes more noticeable when the mushroom is crushed.

habitat: Found in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly associated with oak trees in a beneficial root partnership called mycorrhiza. Look for them in well-drained soil under mature hardwoods, often appearing in small scattered groups rather than large clusters. They prefer areas with rich leaf litter and good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found in spring, though mycelium may be actively growing underground in preparation for summer fruiting.
seasonality.summer: Prime fruiting season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of warm rain. Fresh specimens show the clearest corrugated cap patterns.
seasonality.fall: Peak season continues through early fall, with mushrooms often larger and more robust. Look for them after autumn rains but before hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: No fresh specimens appear, but dried remains may persist on the forest floor as learning specimens.

funFact: The white 'milk' that flows from this mushroom is actually a specialized defense system - it contains compounds that can deter insects and small animals from eating the fungus, essentially acting like a natural pesticide that the mushroom produces on demand when threatened.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other large milkcaps, but the deeply corrugated cap surface is usually distinctive enough to separate it from smooth-capped relatives. Remember the simple trick: if it doesn't look like corrugated cardboard on top and doesn't bleed white milk when cut, it's not a corrugated-cap milky.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Lactarius to Lactifluus based on DNA studies, so older field guides may list it as Lactarius corrugis. Both names refer to the same mushroom, but the scientific community now recognizes the newer classification.
compareHints: Unlike the smooth-capped Weeping Milk Cap which has a velvety texture, the corrugated-cap milky's wrinkled surface is unmistakable. The Peppery Milkcap has a burning hot taste to its milk, while the corrugated-cap's milk is mild. The Deceptive Milky lacks the distinctive corrugated pattern and typically grows much larger. SAFETY NOTE: Never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification - even edible species can cause illness if misidentified or improperly prepared.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the weeping milk cap which has a strong fishy odor and orange-staining milk, the hygrophorus milkcap has mild smell and white milk that stays white.

Among its Lactifluus relatives in New England, the Weeping Milk Cap stands out for producing far more latex than species like the Peppery Milkcap, and lacks the pure white coloring of the Deceptive Milky.
Among its Lactifluus relatives, the Deceptive Milky stands out for its large size and velvety stem texture.
